faq.a: Only if there is a pre‑existing condition (e.g., chronic hypertension) that suddenly worsens; true de‑novo preeclampsia starts after 20 weeks.
No. In the 2019 WHO criteria, any severe feature (e.g., thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, cerebral symptoms) can substitute for proteinuria.
They cross the placenta and can cause fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, and neonatal hypotension.

exam: A 28‑year‑old primigravida at 32 weeks presents with BP 158/108 mmHg and mild edema. What is your next step? — Assess for proteinuria or severe features; if absent, diagnose gestational hypertension and monitor, but plan close surveillance.

A patient with known HIV on ART develops sudden visual disturbances and BP 170/115 mmHg. Which investigation is essential and why? — Urine protein test to confirm preeclampsia; proteinuria confirms diagnosis and guides urgency of delivery.

Why is magnesium sulfate preferred over diazepam for seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia? — Magnesium stabilizes neuronal membranes and reduces cerebral vasospasm; diazepam does not prevent seizures and may depress respiration.

In a low‑resource clinic without lab access, how would you diagnose severe preeclampsia? — Rely on clinical criteria: BP ≥160/110 mmHg plus any severe symptom (headache, epigastric pain, reduced urine output) and bedside dip‑stick protein ≥1+.

A woman at 36 weeks with preeclampsia has platelets 95 × 10⁹/L and AST 80 U/L. What is the most appropriate delivery plan? — Plan for induction or cesarean depending on cervical favorability; severe features mandate delivery within 24‑48 h.

Explain why chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia carries higher maternal risk than de‑novo preeclampsia. — Baseline vascular damage predisposes to placental ischemia, renal insufficiency, and cerebrovascular events, increasing morbidity.

What are the key components of fluid management in severe preeclampsia? — Strict input‑output charting, avoid fluid overload, give diuretics only if pulmonary edema develops, and monitor serum electrolytes.
How does malaria infection increase preeclampsia risk? — Parasite‑induced endothelial activation and anemia amplify placental hypoxia, precipitating hypertensive disorders.
ai.title: Preeclampsia
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy‑specific hypertensive disorder after 20 weeks gestation, marked by new hypertension and proteinuria or organ dysfunction. Early recognition, severity staging, and timely delivery are lifesaving.

b: Onset ≥20 weeks gestation
BP ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions 4 h apart
sections.p: Preeclampsia affects 2‑8 % of pregnancies worldwide and is a leading cause of maternal mortality in low‑resource settings. It reflects abnormal placental development leading to systemic endothelial injury.

b: Severe: BP ≥160/110 mmHg, platelets <100 × 10⁹/L, creatinine >1.1 mg/dL, etc.
Early‑onset carries higher maternal/fetal risk
sections.p: Severity is staged by the presence of severe features (e.g., BP ≥160/110 mmHg, thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, cerebral symptoms). The disease is categorized as mild or severe, and as early‑onset (<34 weeks) or late‑onset (≥34 weeks).

b: Common triggers: chronic hypertension, renal disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, multiple gestation
Tropical contributors: malaria infection, severe anemia, herbal remedies with vasoactive compounds
sections.p: In East African hospitals, co‑morbidities such as HIV, malaria, sickle cell disease, and chronic hypertension increase risk and may mask or worsen presentation.
When a test is unavailable (e.g., protein‑creatinine ratio), use a dipstick ≥1+ as a pragmatic substitute.

t.b: Confirms hypertension; trend helps gauge severity and response to therapy
Identifies thrombocytopenia (<100 × 10⁹/L) and anemia; low platelets signal severe disease
Assesses renal function; creatinine >1.1 mg/dL indicates renal involvement
Elevated >2 × upper limit suggests hepatic involvement
Elevated levels support diagnosis but not essential
Evaluates growth restriction and amniotic fluid; essential when delivery timing is considered

b: Antihypertensives: IV labetalol or hydralazine for BP ≥160/110 mmHg; avoid ACE inhibitors and ARBs in pregnancy
Magnesium sulfate: 4‑g loading dose IV then 1‑g/hr maintenance to prevent seizures; monitor reflexes and respiratory rate
Delivery: definitive treatment; route depends on gestational age, cervical status, and maternal stability
Supportive care: fluid balance, treat seizures, monitor urine output, and correct electrolytes
sections.p: Goal: prevent maternal complications and optimize fetal outcome. Stabilize mother, treat severe hypertension, and deliver when benefits outweigh risks.

b: Gestational hypertension (no proteinuria or severe features)
Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia (new proteinuria or worsening BP)
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (severe hepatic dysfunction, hypoglycemia)
HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) – a severe variant of preeclampsia
sections.p: Conditions that mimic preeclampsia or share features.

b: Proteinuria may be absent early; severe features can still be present
BP may be normal between spikes; repeated measurements are essential
Platelet count can be normal early in severe disease
sections.p: Lab and clinical findings may be falsely reassuring.

b: Always ask about visual disturbances, epigastric pain, and reduced fetal movements
Check for reflex hyper‑reflexia and clonus – early signs of impending seizure
In low‑resource settings, a bedside urine dip‑stick is acceptable for protein detection

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden epigastric or right upper quadrant pain
